'''''Trifolium squamosum''''', usually called '''sea clover''' in English, is an annual herb in the [[Fabaceae|pea family]] that is found close to the Atlantic and Mediterranean shores of Europe. It grows on patches of bare ground in saltmarsh, grassland or open woodland from sea level up to about {{Convert|1,000|m}} towards the southern edge of its range. It is palatable to livestock but has no economic uses.

==Description==
Sea clover is an annual [[herbaceous plant|herb]] which forms patches up to about {{Convert|1|m|ft|0}} in diameter by {{Convert|20-30|cm|frac=2}} high. It has fibrous roots and numerous ascending to erect branched stems which are hairy when young, soon becoming glabrous.

The leaves are arranged alternately along the stems (except the uppermost pair), with a prominent green [[stipule]] up to 10 mm long at the base of each [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]. The leaves, like those of other clovers, are divided into three segments but are distinctive in being narrower than in most other species, being approximately oblong in shape, ca. 20 mm x 8 mm, with a small point at the tip. The leaves have translucent veins and are covered with appressed soft, simple hairs.
[[File:Trifolium squamosum stipule Graveney.jpg|thumb|Sea clover stipules]]

Flowering occurs in early summer, April to July in Britain. The oval flowerheads are terminal, subtended by an opposite pair of leaves, and either stalkless or on a short peduncle up to 0.5 cm long. Each head contains 20–30 small flowers consisting of a green calyx and pink corolla. The calyx can be hairy or glabrous, with a 5 mm long whitish tube with 10 prominent veins, ending in 5 green triangular lobes, the lower one being considerably longer than the upper four. The corolla is about 7 mm long, made up of 5 petals in the characteristic [[Fabaceae|pea-flower]] shape with a hooded standard, two wings and the two lower petals fused to form the keel. There are 10 [[stamen]]s bearing yellow anthers and one style with a brown [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]].
[[File:Trifolium squamosum Graveney leaf.jpg|thumb|Each leaf has three narrow, stalkless, obovate leaflets]]

After flowering, the calyx teeth curve outwards, giving the fruiting heads a starry appearance. The fruit is an obovoid legume about 2.5 mm long containing round seeds about 2 mm in diameter.<ref name=Sell2009>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 3 |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=Stace2019>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=C & M Floristics |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |edition=4th |location=Middlewood Green}}</ref>
[[File:Trifolium squamosum Graveney.jpg|thumb|Details of the calyx in flower and fruit]]

==Taxonomy==
Sea clover was first recognised as a new species by [[Thomas Johnson (botanist)|Thomas Johnson]], who found it in a saltmarsh at [[Borough of Dartford|Dartford]] on 10<sup>th</sup> June 1633 and named it ''Trifolium stellatum glabrum'', or "smooth starrie-headed trefoile'", in his revised edition of [[John Gerard|Gerard's]] Herball that same year.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gerard |first=John |url=https://archive.org/details/gri_33125012606592/page/n1251 |title=The Herball, or, Generall Historie of Plantes, very much enlarged and amended by Thomas Johnson |publisher=Adam Islip, Joice Norton & Richard Whitakers |year=1633 |page=1208}}</ref><ref name=Kitchener2025>{{Cite book |last=Kitchener |first=Mr G. D. |year=2025 |url=https://archive.org/details/kent-rpr-2025/page/n1231 |title=Kent Rare Plant Register}}</ref>

[[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] was impressed by the work of the early British botanists, especially [[Johann Jacob Dillenius|Dillenius]], who had produced, in his opinion, the most perfect ("''perfectissima''") Flora in his edition of [[John Ray]]'s ''Synopsis methodica stirpium Britannicarum'' in 1724, so in 1759 he published a list of the plants of "Anglia" (Britain and Ireland) in his book ''Amoenitates Academicae'' (vol. 4, p. 105).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linnaei |first=Carolus |url=http://archive.org/details/mobot31753000806403 |title=Amoenitates academicae seu Dissertationes variae physicae, medicae, botanicae |publisher=Laurenth Salvii |year=1759}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Ray |first=John |url=https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/13665 |title=Synopsis methodica stirpium Britannicarum |publisher=Gulielmi & Joannis Innys |year=1724 |location=London}}</ref> This included, from Dillenius's Flora, Johnson's smooth starrie clover, which he renamed ''Trifolium squamosum.'' This name takes precedence because it is a properly formulated binomial, unlike Johnson's earlier polynomial. The epithet ''squamosum'' means "scaly", but Linnaeus provided no explanation.

[[William Hudson (botanist)|William Hudson]] was probably unaware of when he called sea clover ''Trifolium maritimum'', or ''Trifolium spicis villosis globosis, calycibus patulis aequalibus, caule adscendente foliolis cuneiformibus hirsutis'' ("the trefoil with hairy globose spikes, equal gaping calyces, ascending stem and wedge-shaped hairy leaves") in his ''Flora Anglica'' in 1762.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hudson |first1=William |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/217308 |title=Flora Anglica: exhibens plantas per regnum angliae sponte crescentes, distributas secundum systema sexuale: cum differentiis specierum, synonymis autorum, nominibus incolarum, solo locorum, tempore florendi, officinalibus pharmacopaeorum |last2=Hudson |first2=William |date=1762 |publisher=Impensis auctoris |location=Londini}}</ref> As this was three years after Linnaeus's list, it stands only as the first synonym, of which there are now many.

''Trifolium squamosum'' has a [[ploidy|chromosome number]] of 2''n'' = 16.<ref name="Stace2019" /> It is not known to hybridise with any other plants<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref> and it has no currently accepted subspecies.<ref name=powo>{{Cite web |title=Trifolium squamosum L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:523726-1 |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

==Distribution and status==
The native range of sea clover is along the Atlantic coasts of Europe, from Britain to Spain and in the western Mediterranean, including North Africa, becoming rare beyond Greece and into the Black Sea. It is generally coastal but extends inland in parts of France, Spain and Greece. It is considered an introduction further north, in Belgium, Germany and the former Czechoslovakia, and it has been established in some remote parts of the world, including California and southern Australia.<ref name="powo" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Trifolium squamosum L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/5359194 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref>

Its global threat status has not been evaluated,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |access-date=23 December 2025}}</ref> but in England and Wales it is classified as LC ([[Least concern species|least concern]]) on the grounds that it is not declining, although its range has decreased dramatically since the 1930s and losses are continuing.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.w4g |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref> One author has calculated that it has declined by 49% in less than a century.<ref name="Kitchener2025"/> Previously, it was considered nationally scarce on the basis that there were only 60 hectads (dots on the map) for it in the 1990s.<ref name=Stewart1994>{{cite book |last1=Stewart |first1=A. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Preston |first3=C.D. |title=Scarce Plants in Britain |date=1994 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref> A study of clovers in the Mediterranean classified it as very common in Greece, common in Portugal, Spain, France and Italy, and rare in Croatia.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=The genus Trifolium (Fabaceae) in south Europe: a critical review on species richness and distribution | last1=Scoppola |first1=A. |journal=Nordic Journal of Botany |pages=1–17 |year=2018 | volume=36 | article-number=njb-01723 |url=https://nsojournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1111/njb.01723 |language=en |doi=10.1111/njb.01723 | bibcode=2018NorJB..36.1723S |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Where it occurs in England and Wales it is classified as an [[axiophyte]], which means it is of nature conservation importance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/learn/getting-started/terms/general-terms/axiophytes |access-date=2025-12-23 |website=bsbi.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Kitchener2025"/>

==Habitat and ecology==
In Britain, sea clover grows mostly in coastal areas, typically in grassy upper saltmarsh habitats. With its upright growth habit, it is not tolerant of heavy grazing or mowing and, because it is an annual, it tends to grow on patches of bare ground. This makes it difficult to describe a vegetation community: most of its sites are probably in upper saltmarsh communities such as [[Juncus maritimus|sea rush]] swards (A2.532 in the EUNIS habitat system), [[Elymus athericus|sea couch]] saltmarsh ([[British NVC community SM24|SM24]] in the [[British National Vegetation Classification|NVC]]) or [[Lolium arundinaceum|tall fescue]] grassland ([[British NVC community MG12|MG12]]) (although it was not recorded at all in the NVC project) but it seems to occur in disturbed areas which are not typical of the habitat.<ref name=Rodwell>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities, vols. 1-5 |date=1991–2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref> It is considered a [[Raunkiær_plant_life-form#Therophytes|therophyte]], which means that it grows quickly to exploit its niche and produces its seeds early in the year.<ref name="Plantatt">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=M.O. |last2=Preston |first2=C.D. |last3=Roy |first3=D.B. |title=PLANTATT - Attributes of British and Irish Plants - Spreadsheet |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/biblio/plantatt-attributes-british-and-irish-plants-spreadsheet |publisher=UK Biological Records Centre}}</ref>

The most likely place to find it in modern Britain is behind sea defences, particularly in the estuaries of the Thames and Severn. Here, it often grows along the side of the access track that often traces the landward edge of the sea wall. The disturbance associated with roads and tracks also accounts for its presence in inland sites, although it does not tend to persist.<ref name=Crouch>{{Cite book |last=H.J. Crouch |url=http://archive.org/details/trifolium-squamosum-in-somerset |title=Trifolium Squamosum In Somerset |date=2021-02-20}}</ref><ref name="Kitchener2025"/>

Further south sea clover is much less restricted to coastal areas. In Greece, for instance, it grows in fields, grasslands and forests up to {{Convert|1,000|m|abbr=on}} above sea level.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fotiadis |first1=G. |last2=Vrahnakis |first2=M.S. |last3=Merou |first3=Th. |last4=Vidakis |first4=K. |date=2010 |title=Ecology, chorology and commonness of the Trifolium taxa in Greece |journal=Feddes Repertorium |volume=121 |issue=1–2 |pages=66–68 |doi=10.1002/fedr.200911129}}</ref>

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg-type indicator values]] are L=9, F=6, R=6, N=7 and S=2, which show that it has a preference for bright sunlight, slightly (or seasonally) damp conditions, neutral pH, low fertility and some salinity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tichý |first1=Lubomír |last2=Axmanová |first2=Irena |last3=Dengler |first3=Jürgen |last4=Guarino |first4=Riccardo |last5=Jansen |first5=Florian |last6=Midolo |first6=Gabriele |last7=Nobis |first7=Michael P. |last8=Van Meerbeek |first8=Koenraad |last9=Aćić |first9=Svetlana |last10=Attorre |first10=Fabio |last11=Bergmeier |first11=Erwin |last12=Biurrun |first12=Idoia |last13=Bonari |first13=Gianmaria |last14=Bruelheide |first14=Helge |last15=Campos |first15=Juan Antonio |year=2023 |title=Ellenberg-type indicator values for European vascular plant species |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jvs.13168 |journal=Journal of Vegetation Science |volume=34 |issue=1 |article-number=e13168 |doi=10.1111/jvs.13168 |bibcode=2023JVegS..34E3168T |issn=1100-9233|hdl=11585/918013 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Plantatt"/>

A few insects pests have been identified in Europe,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trifolium squamosum – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superrosids/rosids/fabids/fabales/fabaceae/faboideae/trifolieae/trifolium/trifolium-squamosum/ |access-date=2025-12-24 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref> but none in Britain yet:<ref name=redfern2002>{{cite journal |last1=Redfern |first1=Margaret |last2=Shirley |first2=Peter |title=British Plant Galls |journal=Field Studies |date=2002 |volume=10 |pages=207–531 |isbn=1-85153-214-5}}</ref>

* the weevil ''Protapion difforme'' feeds on this plant;
* the larvae of the beetle ''Bruchidius pygmaeus'' bore into the seeds;
* the scale insect ''Pseudococcus aridorum'' lives on the stems.

One type of fungus, ''Uromyces fallens'', has been recorded causing pustules on the leaves.
